implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue (since 1.5) is the standard in-process realization: take() removes exactly one element and waits when empty, put() waits when the capacity is reached, implementations are thread-safe, and insertion happens-before removal, so several consumer threads may compete while each element reaches exactly one of them - the javadoc's own usage example starts two consumer threads on one queue. LinkedBlockingQueue is the usual choice; the brokered JMS Queue is the sibling when the channel must outlive the JVM.
pitfalls: Interruption is the only clean stop signal for a blocked take(); swallowing InterruptedException clears the flag and leaves shutdown wedged.
new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() is unbounded by default - the classic way this pattern converts overload into OutOfMemoryError.
BlockingQueue has no close operation (the javadoc suggests poison objects), so end-of-stream must be designed explicitly.

variants.name: JMS / Jakarta Messaging queue on a broker
variants.implementation_notes: The classic brokered realization: a Queue object names a provider-side channel and Session.createConsumer(queue) creates a receiver whose receive()/onMessage() obtains messages the provider holds until acknowledgement - including while the consumer process is down. Two consumers created on the same queue are competing consumers by definition; each message goes to one of them, and the provider, not the application, owns redelivery and dead-letter handling. The JMS API explicitly leaves retention time and overflow consequences to the provider, so those policies must be configured and tested rather than assumed.
pitfalls: receive() with no timeout blocks indefinitely when the connection dies mid-poll; use a timeout or an async listener with reconnect logic.
Acknowledging before the work completes (auto-ack) loses messages on crash; acknowledging afterwards makes redelivery an idempotency problem.
The API does not define queue length or overflow behaviour - a provider that silently drops or blocks must be a deliberate, tested choice.
